newsitem.title: USA: CME study backs S&P 500 split to draw small users.
newsitem.headline: CME study backs S&P 500 split to draw small users.

text.p: A study commissioned by the Chicago Mercantile Exchange concluded that reducing the size of the Standard & Poor's 500 futures contract would encourage use by new and smaller customers and also let large users fine-tune their hedges.

The study, completed February 11 and distributed late Tuesday at a members' meeting, said the case was less clear for also doubling the minimum tick size to 0.10 index point from its current 0.05 to keep its dollar value at $25.
The study was conducted by Roger Huang and Hans Stoll of Vanderbilt University's Financial Markets Research Center.

Currently, S&P 500 futures are priced at $500 times the index value. The study said the underlying dollar value has grown more than five-fold since the S&P 500 futures opened in April 1982, making it much bigger than other futures contracts and "increasingly inaccessible to smaller investors."
The study said halving the multiplier to $250 from $500 would be the easiest of the three ways it cited to make the contract size comparable to other stock index products.
One alternative would be to replace the current index with a new index one-half the value of the existing contract.
Another option would be to add a supplemental mini-contract to trade in addition to the existing contract, but this approach would risk fragmenting liquidity, the study said.

The authors said splitting the contract would require a decision on whether to change the minimum tick size. If the contract size were halved but the tick size left at 0.05, the dollar value of each tick would drop to $12.50. Doubling the tick size to 0.10 point would keep the dollar value at $25.
CME has not yet decided whether to act on the conclusions. "There might be a recommendation in about 60 days, but we're very much in an analytical mode," a spokeswoman said.

Any changes to the contract would require action by the CME's board, but the spokeswoman was unsure whether they would need approval from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. ((DerivativesDesk(312)408-8750/E-mail:derivatives@reuters.com))
